content: Essential medicines are defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as drugs that meet the healthcare needs of the majority of the population. These medicines should always be available in sufficient quantities, in appropriate dosage forms, and at a price that is affordable for the community. The WHO has developed a model list of essential medicines, and each country is encouraged to create its own list based on local healthcare priorities. Currently, more than 150 countries have published their own official lists of essential medicines. The WHO's model list is divided into two sections: the core list and the complementary list. The core list includes the minimum set of medicines required for a basic healthcare system. These medicines are selected based on their proven efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness for treating priority health conditions. Priority conditions are identified based on their current and anticipated public health significance, as well as the potential for safe and cost-effective treatment. The complementary list includes essential medicines for treating priority diseases that require specialized diagnostic or monitoring facilities. Medicines may also be included in the complementary list if they are associated with consistently higher costs or less favorable cost-effectiveness in various healthcare settings. The creation of an essential medicines list allows health authorities, particularly in developing countries, to make the best use of their pharmaceutical resources.
